title: Saving for a Home Down Payment: Strategy and Milestones
content:
Purchasing a primary residence is frequently the largest single financial transaction an individual will undertake. Preparing for homeownership requires structured saving not just for the down payment, but also for closing costs, inspection fees, and initial moving reserves.

A common myth is that home buyers must put down 20% in cash. Conventional mortgages allow down payments as low as 3% to 5%, while FHA loans accommodate 3.5%. However, putting down less than 20% on a conventional mortgage requires paying Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)—a monthly fee that protects the lender against default without benefiting the borrower. Furthermore, a larger down payment reduces monthly interest payments and establishes instant home equity.

In addition to the down payment, buyers must budget for closing costs, which typically range between 2% and 5% of the total loan amount. These fees cover loan origination, title insurance, appraisal, escrow fees, and property taxes.

Because home purchase timelines are typically short-to-medium term (1 to 4 years), down payment funds should be insulated from stock market fluctuations. Allocating home savings to Treasury bills, certificates of deposit, or high-yield savings accounts guarantees your capital is fully available when the right property arrives.
